title: Why is English full of French words?

entries.note: Considered as the French for 'unravelled' in the show's intro; it means to untie and gave English [[gave:dénouement]].
Comes from French [[from:dénouer]], to untie.
Used as an example: the only French-derived word in Rob's sentence, showing that everyday speech stays mostly Germanic.
One of the only French words among the top 100 English words in everyday use.
Another of the few French words among the 100 most-used English words, alongside [[see:people]].
Also called William the Bastard, the Duke of Normandy who became king in 1066 and replaced the Anglo-Saxon nobles and bishops with Normans.
Conventionally begins after the Battle of Hastings because of the influx of French, though the real change was gradual, from about 1150 to 1500.
The Germanic English spoken before the Battle of Hastings; it was full of hl- words and its poetry alliterated instead of rhyming.
Itself a French word, mentioned while describing William replacing the Anglo-Saxon nobility.
An Anglo-Saxon title used before the French titles such as [[see:barons]] and [[see:dukes]] arrived.
An Anglo-Saxon title from before the Norman titles arrived.
One of the French titles that came in with the Norman nobility.
One of the French titles that came in with the Norman nobility.
One of the French titles that came in with the Norman nobility.
One of the French titles that came in with the Norman nobility.
The only Anglo-Saxon bishop that [[see:William the Conqueror]] did not sack.
A French legal word that came in when the Normans took control of the courts.
A French legal word that came in under Norman rule.
A French legal word that came in under Norman rule.
A French legal word that came in under Norman rule.
A French legal word that came in under Norman rule, replacing or sitting alongside Anglo-Saxon words.
Contrasted with Germanic [[see:food]] to show the Norman power dynamic.
The Germanic counterpart of French [[see:cuisine]].
Has a Germanic name in the field but becomes French-derived [[see:beef]] on the plate.
The French name for the meat of a [[see:cow]]; [[see:Ivanhoe]] makes the same joke.
Germanic animal name paired with French [[see:mutton]] for the meat.
The French-derived word for [[see:sheep]] meat; it goes back to Gaulish [[from:mouton]].
Germanic animal name that becomes [[see:pork]] on the table.
The French-derived word for [[see:pig]] meat; it shows up again in [[see:porcupine]].
Germanic animal name that becomes French-derived [[see:poultry]] on the table.
The French-derived word used for [[see:chicken]] as food.
Germanic animal name paired with French-derived [[see:venison]].
The French-derived word for [[see:deer]] meat.
Walter Scott's 1819 novel, in which the jester Wamba jokes that the Saxon ox becomes French [[see:beef]] when it is eaten.
An alteration of the French word now spelled [[same-root:maison]]; like [[see:house]] it means house, but it is the fancy one.
The Germanic word paired with French-derived [[see:mansion]].
A French word for a meal, an example of the wealthy Normans' food vocabulary.
Mentioned with [[see:supper]] as words for the extra meals of wealthy French speakers.
Mentioned with [[see:dinner]] as words for the extra meals of wealthy French speakers.
One of the Germanic words for close family; combined with French in [[see:grandfather]].
One of the Germanic words for immediate family.
A Germanic close-family word; its gh once stood for a ch sound that the Normans found uncomfortable.
One of the Germanic words for immediate family.
One of the Germanic words for immediate family.
One of the Germanic words for immediate family.
A hybrid of French grand and Germanic [[from:father]].
A French word for extended family; such words mattered mainly to nobles interested in genealogy and dynasties.
A French word for extended family, reflecting the Norman nobility's interest in lineage.
A French word for extended family, reflecting the Norman nobility's interest in lineage.
A French word for extended family, reflecting the Norman nobility's interest in lineage.
A French word; peasants handing down a farmstead didn't need words for distant relatives such as cousins.
Also called the Angevin dynasty; this French dynasty followed the [[see:Normans]] and spoke a central French dialect closer to modern French.
Essentially Norsemen who had settled in northern France; they ruled England and brought [[see:Norman French]].
A rather Germanic variety of French that kept W sounds, which became G in central French, as in [[see:warden]] versus [[see:guardian]].
Borrowed from Norman French with a W; a doublet of [[same-root:guardian]].
Borrowed from the later central French of the [[see:Plantagenets]] with a G; a doublet of [[same-root:warden]].
The Celtic language of the Gauls in pre-Roman France; the Romans suppressed it so thoroughly that only a few words survive in French.
The French word for lark, one of the few words that survive from [[from:Gaulish]].
A Gaulish survival in French meaning sheep, which gave English [[gave:mutton]].
The French word for heather, a survival from [[from:Gaulish]].
The French word for a path or road, a survival from [[from:Gaulish]].
The descendants of Latin spoken in the Roman strongholds of Spain, France, Portugal, Romania and Italy.
Rob's term for the Latin varieties the [[see:Romance languages]] descend from; he is unsure whether it's still an acceptable name.
Romano-British Latin must have existed, but almost no trace of it survives, unlike Latin in France.
Like Parisian French, it is one dialect that came to be called simply the national language.
The Spanish of the royal family, now just called Spanish, a parallel to Parisian French.
A Germanic tribe that settled in northern Gaul after Rome fell and influenced French.
Comes from a French dialect with a C sound; a double borrowing with [[same-root:château]].
Comes from a French dialect with a CH sound; a double borrowing with [[same-root:castle]].
A C/CH double borrowing alongside [[same-root:chattel]].
A C/CH double borrowing alongside [[same-root:cattle]].
The group of northern French languages, named after their word for yes; contrasted with southern [[see:langue d'oc]].
Southern French languages, named after oc, their word for yes.
A newer borrowing from French that kept its French spelling and so sounds French.
A newer borrowing from French that kept its French spelling.
Keeps the S of Old French estat; modern French lost the S, while English lost the initial E.
A relic of Old French es- words; modern French has [[same-root:étage]].
Given as the Old French-style form behind [[same-root:state]].
Shows the tip that a French é often stands for a lost S: add an S and you get English [[same-root:stage]].
The 'little hat' on French vowels, added in a spelling reform to mark a removed S, as in [[see:hotel]] versus [[see:hostel]].
Borrowed from French when it still had its S; a double borrowing with [[same-root:hotel]].
From French hôtel, whose circumflex marks the lost S of [[same-root:hostel]]; the two are a double borrowing.
Another word where the French circumflex marks a lost S, like [[see:hotel]].
Its gh was once a ch sound that the Normans found uncomfortable, as with [[see:daughter]].
An example of a gh spelling that replaced an earlier ch-like sound after the Normans arrived.
Began with an H in Old English, as [[from:hlāford]]; the Normans couldn't manage initial hl-, so it disappeared.
Borrowed from French, where it marked removed letters, from Greek for 'turned away'; the possessive apostrophe marks a dropped E.
The Old English-style possessive, once spelled with -es; contrasted with the French-style [[see:the sword of the knight]].
A recorded construction often used to explain the possessive [[see:apostrophe]]; the hosts call that explanation incorrect overcompensation.
A Canterbury Tales phrase where 'ladys' showed possession without an [[see:apostrophe]]; modern editions add one.
The possessive with 'of' is a construction copied from French, alongside the Old English [[see:the knight's sword]].
The French for knight, from cheval, horse, and borrowed into English repeatedly as [[same-root:cavalry]], [[same-root:chivalry]] and [[same-root:cavalier]].
One of several borrowings of the same French word, ultimately from cheval, horse.
A Norman-era borrowing from the same horse word as [[same-root:cavalry]] and [[same-root:cavalier]].
Another borrowing of the French word for a horseman, related to [[same-root:chevalier]].
The phrase [[from:avant-garde]] after it went through English processing.
The French phrase that, borrowed earlier, gave [[gave:vanguard]].
An earlier borrowing of the same French word for boss as [[same-root:chef]].
A later borrowing of the French for boss, made in an era keen on French culinary words; a doublet of [[same-root:chief]].
Comes from the same French source as [[same-root:parson]].
A doublet of [[same-root:person]].
A borrowing of the French for small, doubled by [[same-root:petite]].
A later borrowing of the French for small; a doublet of [[same-root:petty]].
A doublet of [[same-root:etiquette]], from the French for a label.
French for a label; it came to mean exclusive court rules under [[see:Louis XIV]], possibly copied from Spanish royalty. A doublet of [[same-root:ticket]].
The Sun King, at whose court the concept of [[see:etiquette]] arose.
A doublet of [[same-root:loyal]].
A doublet of [[same-root:legal]].
A doublet of [[same-root:royal]].
A doublet of [[same-root:regal]].
The French word for nice, borrowed four times into English: [[gave:genteel]], [[gave:gentle]], [[gave:gentile]] and [[gave:jaunty]].
One of four English borrowings of French [[from:gentil]].
One of four English borrowings of French [[from:gentil]].
Meaning a non-Jewish person, it comes from the same French source, [[from:gentil]].
The surprising fourth borrowing of French [[from:gentil]].
Ultimately from the same French source as [[same-root:feast]] and [[same-root:festival]].
A French word for a meal, sharing a source with [[same-root:fete]] and [[same-root:festival]].
Shares its ultimate French source with [[same-root:fete]] and [[same-root:feast]].
From French joie; it came in independently of related words like [[see:enjoy]].
From French jolie; ultimately related to [[same-root:joy]].
One of the joy words that came from French at different times, independently of [[same-root:joy]].
A whole French phrase borrowed wholesale into English.
An example of a newer borrowing that still sounds and looks French.
An example of a newer, French-looking borrowing.
Borrowed during the 1700s fashion for French words.
A 1700s borrowing that English speakers pronounce terribly.
Borrowed during the 1700s mania for French words.
Borrowed during the 1700s mania for French words.
Literally 'bottom of the bag', with [[see:cul]] meaning arse; first a medical word for a diverticulum, then for a dead-end road.
The Germanic term Rob prefers to [[see:cul-de-sac]].
The first element of [[see:cul-de-sac]]; a rude French word for the backside.
Literally means 'chewed paper', mâché meaning chewed, though fortunately it's not literal in most cases.
Now a live-in nanny, originally a name for the arrangement, meaning 'on equal footing': room and board in exchange for work.
Called self-explanatory: literally head to head.
A person's social environment, from a French word for the middle of something; used mainly by people trying to sound snooty.
A pretentious substitute for 'mix', which is all it means in French.
A Derby restaurant menu offered 'strawberry gâteaux', with the French plural X, but served only one cake.
In French a union, and also the linking of a silent final consonant to the next word, as in [[see:beaux-arts]]; it makes spoken French sound like word soup.
An example of [[see:liaison]], where the normally silent X of beaux is pronounced before arts.
Just the French for ask; English gave it extra forcefulness so it could sit alongside [[see:ask]].
The native word that French-derived [[see:demand]] sits beside.
Jess finds that in English it suggests a sticky situation, while in French it is a collapse or disaster.
A Germanic word paired with French-derived [[see:respond]], which has a slightly different nuance.
A French-derived near-synonym of [[see:answer]].
A Germanic word paired with French-derived [[see:desire]].
A French-derived near-synonym of [[see:wish]].
A Germanic word paired with French-derived [[see:commence]].
A French-derived near-synonym of [[see:begin]].
A Germanic word paired with French-derived [[see:regard]].
A French-derived near-synonym of [[see:look]], often a bit more poncy.
In French it is the past participle of 'to risk' and also carries the same racy sense as in English.
A French adjective applied to the Anglo-Saxon noun brain, perhaps because of medicine's love of foreign words.
A French adjective used for the Anglo-Saxon noun house.
A French-derived adjective used for the Anglo-Saxon noun town.
A French verb meaning to remember or come to mind, which English turned into a noun for something you buy.
A French borrowing of jogging, which Rob finds questionable; the French also say [[see:le footing]].
An even worse French word for jogging that Rob hates; the French like -ing words for their English twang.
The French word for a car park, one of their English-sounding -ing words.
A French -ing borrowing that Rob finds acceptable, since English says shopping too.
An egregious French borrowing, ironic because the planing comes from a French word for glide.
When a language takes back a word it lent to another, as French did with [[see:tennis]].
French re-borrowed it for the sport and for trainers, though the name comes from French [[from:tenez]].
French for a trainer, short for basketball shoe.
Meaning 'take it' or 'hold it', shouted when hitting the ball; it gave the name [[gave:tennis]].
Literally a stoker of a steam engine, because the first cars were steam-driven, from French chauffer, to warm.
In English, flair; it was a French word for a tuft or plume of feathers worn on a hat.
A French drink of beer mixed with lemonade, the same as a [[equivalent:shandy]] or [[equivalent:Radler]].
The English name for beer mixed with lemonade; ordering one in England is somewhat unacceptable.
The German name for beer with lemonade, perfectly acceptable to order in Germany.
The American iced tea and lemonade drink; Jess jokes about a stronger 'Arnold Schwarzenegger Palmer'.
From French bouder, to pout or sulk: a lady's private 'sulking room'; ladyfinger biscuits are called boudoirs in French.
Discussed in earlier episodes; it means throwing your wooden shoe into machinery and is related to [[same-root:sabaton]].
Said to be related to [[same-root:sabotage]].
A political coup is always short for [[from:coup d'état]]; in French the word means a blow, strike, cut or slap.
Before this phrase, [[see:coup]] meant any blow or strike with no political sense.
Something cut off, a piece you cut from something else, related to [[same-root:coup]].
French for a punch, poing being the fist; another use of [[see:coup]].
French for a kick, another use of [[see:coup]].
Originally three French words, de bon air: of good appearance or lineage, like putting on airs.
From Old French [[from:pied de grue]], crane's foot, after the forked symbol showing descent in genealogical charts.
From Old French [[from:couvre-feu]], cover fire: a bell signalled time to bank fires, which were covered with a lidded firecover overnight.
A French word, used for the poor Anglo-Saxons, which just means country people.
From French porc espin, spiny or thorny pig; another appearance of the [[see:pork]] word.
A word for a random mix, never spelled consistently, with French precursors such as [[from:hotchpot]].
An Anglo-French legal term for pooling a group's property so it could be divided equally; also food shaken in a pot.
Literally means 'rotten pot'; hardly anyone has it now because of plug-in air fresheners.
Probably from French [[from:pique-nique]], though German has a candidate too; a supposed racist origin is false.
The French spelling a friend mocked in a supermarket, though French had the word before English [[see:picnic]].
English paces sentences by stressed syllables, so 'I want ball' and 'I would want the ball' take the same time; contrasted with [[see:syllable-timed]].
French moves syllable by syllable, which is why Rob has to change rhythm to speak it; contrasted with [[see:stress-timed]].
Spelled like the French word but often treated as if it began with Latin com-; it's closer to [[same-root:camera]], meaning people sharing a chamber.
Related to [[same-root:camaraderie]] through the idea of a chamber.
Spelled differently from [[same-root:camaraderie]], which keeps the French spelling.
Pioneered rhyme in English poetry, a habit taken from French literature; many of his rhymes depend on pronouncing a final E.
